lines.text: In September twenty twenty-three, inside Mexico's Congress, two small boxes were opened in front of the cameras. Inside lay two tiny bodies with long heads and three fingers on each hand.
The man presenting them said, under oath, that they were not human. Not from our evolution. A thousand years old. Found in the desert of Nazca, in Peru.
The clip went around the world in hours. Aliens, shown to a parliament. For millions of people, that sounded like disclosure.
But a parliament is not a laboratory. Science has its own test for an extraordinary claim. You submit it, and experts tear it apart before anyone believes it.
So tonight we do exactly that. We send the Nazca mummies out for peer review. Five referees. One rebuttal from the authors. And then the editor's decision.

First, the submission. The claim, as its authors make it, is simple. In the deserts around Nazca and Palpa, a group of three-fingered beings was found, preserved for over a thousand years. They are not human.
Every paper needs a methods section. Where were the specimens found, by whom, and how? Here the trouble starts. No archaeologist excavated them. Ever.

According to the people who promoted them, the bodies came from huaqueros, tomb looters from Palpa. Their leader was known only as Mario. One of the promoters called him a delinquent, well known to the local police.

In January twenty seventeen, the French explorer Thierry Jamin wrote to Peru's Ministry of Culture. He described about twenty humanoid bodies in stone sarcophagi, with three-fingered hands. Then he raised money online, almost forty thousand euros, to study them.

In June twenty seventeen, a streaming site released a series about the largest body, a pale, white-powdered figure the team called Maria. Gaia, the site, said she might be around seventeen hundred years old.

Six years later, smaller bodies, about sixty centimetres tall, reached Mexico's Congress, presented by the journalist and UFO researcher Jaime Maussan. The claim had grown. Non-human, and possibly intelligent.

Editor's note on the submission. A specimen bought from looters has no context: no grave, no layers, no record. Science can still test it. But every test now has to work twice as hard. Send it to the first referee.
Referee one is a radiologist. Because the strongest card the authors hold is the scans. X-rays and CT scans, published for years, showing skeletons inside the bodies.

And it's true. There are real bones inside. Promoters point to skeletons with no obvious seams, organs, even what they call eggs. To them, that is the end of the argument. To a radiologist, it is the beginning.

Look at Maria first. Anthropologist Andrew Nelson said she looks like a typical Nazca mummy, sitting in the flexed position Nazca people used for their dead. A human being. Wrapped and buried by her family centuries ago.

The hands and feet are where the scans get interesting. Experts reading the images say they show signs of manipulation: digits removed, bones rearranged, and a white powder coating that hides the joins.
Then a three-fingered hand came into the hands of Peru's own forensic institute. The X-rays showed human bones from adults and juveniles. One finger bone had been glued in backwards.
And the eggs? In one sixty centimetre figure seized by Peruvian authorities, the eggs on the scan turned out to be stones.
Reviewer note. A scan shows what is inside. It cannot tell you whether it grew there. Real bones are what you would expect, whether the body is alien, or assembled from real remains.
Referee two is an anatomist. The job: does this body make sense as a living animal? Every vertebrate on Earth follows a plan. Bones meet in predictable ways, because they have to carry weight.

In January twenty twenty-four, forensic archaeologist Flavio Estrada showed what was inside two small figures seized at a Lima courier office, on their way to Mexico. The head of one was the skull of a camelid. A llama or an alpaca.

The arms and legs? Bird bones. The snout of the skull had been cut away, and a face was modelled on the back of the braincase. Metal plates had been placed on the chest, to look mysterious on an X-ray.
Estrada's verdict was blunt. These are not extraterrestrials. Not intraterrestrials. Not a new species. Not hybrids. In his words, they are dolls assembled from the bones of animals from this planet.
He also noted something any anatomist would: there is no evolutionary logic. With those flat feet and those joints, the figures could never have walked, or even stood.
The authors push back. A report by Cliff Miles proposes the small bodies are a brand-new genus and species. And promoters insist the seized figures were cheap folk dolls, not their specimens.

Reviewer note. That objection cuts both ways. If the authors' bodies are different, they must be opened to the same independent test. Until then, the only small figures examined by a state lab were built, not born.
Referee three is a chemist. Forget the bones. What is the skin made of? A body that is a thousand years old should be made of a thousand-year-old body.

Peru's forensic team used infrared spectroscopy, which reads the chemical fingerprint of a material. On the three-fingered hand, they found wool, polypropylene plastic, and a glue so specific they matched it to a brand: UHU.
The so-called skin of the small figures was a paste of glues, plant fibre and ground paper. Estrada's team looked for cells and found none. Just fibre, gum, glue and oils.

Then the white powder. The authors told Congress the beings were buried in diatomaceous earth, fossil algae, and that is what preserved them. Maybe. But a white coat over everything is also exactly how you hide a join.
Reviewer note. Modern synthetic glue cannot be a thousand years old. Whatever is ancient in these objects, the assembly is recent.
Referee four runs a radiocarbon lab. And this is the evidence Congress heard most about: a carbon-fourteen date from Mexico's national university, UNAM, about a thousand years.
Here is what the lab actually did. In May twenty seventeen, a client sent samples which, the client said, were skin and brain tissue. About half a gram. The lab dated them. That was all.

When the date was used in Congress, the university reissued its statement. Its staff never took the samples and never saw the source. It rejects any use or interpretation of its results beyond the date itself.
And think about what an old date means. Peru's desert is full of real burials more than a thousand years old. Old tissue is exactly what you would get from a looted grave.
Reviewer note. Radiocarbon dates the material in the tube, not the object on the table. An ancient date is fully consistent with ancient human remains, reworked today.
Referee five is a geneticist. This is the test that should settle it. Alien life would not share our genetic code. Human remains would.
The promoters' own sequencing has circulated since twenty eighteen, with headlines about unknown DNA. Large shares of the reads could not be matched to anything. That sounded like a smoking gun.

But unknown is not alien. Old, dirty, handled tissue is full of bacteria and broken fragments that databases cannot place. Even the promoters' reports said most identifiable reads were human contamination.
The raw data was public, so anyone could check it. In December twenty twenty-five, bioinformatician Alaina Hardie and Alan Izarraras-Gomez of UNAM published their reanalysis.
Their conclusion: the DNA is unambiguously modern human. It lacks the damage patterns that real ancient DNA always shows. The most likely source is contamination in the lab.
Reviewer note. The genetic signal is human, and modern. Nothing in the published sequence data requires a non-human source.
Now the authors get their right of reply. In November twenty twenty-three, at a second session in Mexico's Congress, a line of doctors testified that the bodies were real, once-living organisms.

In twenty twenty-four, an American lawyer and his team said Maria's fingerprints did not look like human prints. Preliminary, he stressed. In twenty twenty-five, a Russian doctor self-published a CT study arguing the bodies looked biologically consistent.
In January twenty twenty-six, the promoters said six bodies were handed to a university in Ica, which asked for them to be registered as cultural heritage. Research, they say, continues.

And there was a lawsuit. Maussan announced a three hundred million dollar claim against Peru. The court record tells a quieter story: declared inadmissible in twenty twenty-five, rejected on appeal, archived in April twenty twenty-six. It never reached trial.
And the theory keeps moving. In October twenty twenty-six, Maussan floated a new idea: maybe the bodies are humans from the future.
Editor's reading of the rebuttal. It offers many voices, but no one has handed a specimen, with a documented chain of custody, to an independent lab that publishes in a peer-reviewed journal.

There is one more referee the authors never asked for. History. In the nineteenth century, scientists measured Andean skulls to argue that ancient Peruvians were somehow other. The historian Christopher Heaney sees the same pattern here.
Ancient Peruvians built cities, irrigation, and the giant lines in the desert. Every alien story about Nazca quietly takes that achievement away from them, and gives it to someone from the sky.

Peru's mummy experts said it most clearly in twenty seventeen. These finds, they wrote, are without any doubt human remains, the cultural heritage of the nation. One of them added: you cannot take away the condition of human from a human being.

Because that is the part the clip never showed. If the large bodies are real Nazca mummies, they were real people. Someone's grandmother. Someone's child. Taken from their graves and reshaped to sell a story.

Peru has treated it as a crime from the start. Prosecutors opened a case on looted archaeological material in twenty seventeen. One man linked to the first finds was given a suspended sentence in twenty twenty-two.
Five referee reports are in. The authors have replied. Time for the editor's decision.
Here is how the claim scored.

The large bodies are best explained as real ancient human mummies: evidence. The small figures examined by Peru's state lab were built from animal bones: evidence. The three-fingered hand was human bones and glue: evidence. And an old carbon date proves an alien origin: debunked.

Unknown DNA proves a non-human being: debunked, it is modern human contamination. Every specimen independently tested: not yet, still open. And the core claim, non-human beings from Nazca: no evidence.
Decision: rejected. Not because the idea of alien life is silly. It isn't. But because every test this claim could be put through, it failed, and every time it failed, the story changed.
So what do the scans really show? Real bones. Some from humans, some from llamas and birds. Joined with modern glue, wrapped in paper paste, and coated in white powder.
What they don't show is anything that never lived on Earth. The mystery was never in the bodies. It was in how a looted grave can end up in a parliament.
If we ever do find life beyond Earth, it will not arrive in a box from a tomb raider. It will come through the slow, boring, beautiful process you just watched. Submission. Review. Replication.
And the people inside these bodies deserve what every one of us would want. A name, if it can be found. A grave. And to be left in peace.
This has been a case file from Ancient Machines. If you want the next claim sent out for review, tell me in the comments which one. And subscribe, so you don't miss the decision.
